chapter_note.about: The ALU is where the processor does arithmetic. This chapter builds up from the full adder to the ripple-carry adder and its delay, then the carry look-ahead adder that removes the delay. It adds subtraction, overflow and the status flags, then the Booth algorithm for signed multiplication and IEEE floating-point arithmetic. GATE asks few questions here but they are mechanical: simulate the adder, count delay or gates, trace Booth, or decode a float.
chapter_note.simple: The ALU is the calculator inside the processor. Its basic cell is the full adder, which adds one column of binary digits and passes a carry to the next column. A row of them is slow because each column waits for the carry from the column before, so a faster design works out all the carries in advance. Subtracting is adding with the second number flipped and one extra 1. After each operation the ALU also sets flags that say if the answer was zero, negative, carried or overflowed. Multiplication uses a shortcut that handles runs of ones with one subtract and one add. Decimals are stored in a scientific-notation form called floating point. In exam words: full adder, ripple and look-ahead carry, add/subtract and overflow, flags, Booth multiplication, and IEEE 754.

cards.title: Full adder
cards.simple: Adding two numbers on paper goes column by column: add the two digits and the carry from the column on the right, write the last digit, and carry the rest to the left. A full adder is one such column in binary. It takes three bits (A, B and the carry in) and gives two bits: the sum bit to write down and the carry out to pass on. Line up as many full adders as there are columns, and you can add numbers of any width. In exam words: a full adder has S = A⊕B⊕Cin and Cout = A·B + Cin·(A⊕B); it is two half adders plus an OR gate, and n of them in a row make an n-bit adder.
cards.idea: A **full adder** adds three bits (A, B and the carry-in) and outputs a **sum** bit and a **carry-out**. Chain n of them, each carry-out feeding the next stage's carry-in, to add n-bit numbers.
cards.definition:
$$S=A\oplus B\oplus C_{in},\qquad C_{out}=A\cdot B + C_{in}\cdot(A\oplus B)$$

- $A,B$ = the two input bits, $C_{in}$ = carry from the lower stage.
- $S$ = sum bit (1 for an odd number of 1s). $C_{out}$ = 1 when at least two inputs are 1.
- Built from two half adders ($S=A\oplus B$, $C=AB$) and one OR gate.
cards.intuition_full: Count the ones among A, B and Cin. The count can be 0, 1, 2 or 3, which in binary is 00, 01, 10 or 11. The right bit is the sum and the left bit is the carry. The sum bit is 1 for counts 1 and 3, which is the parity, A⊕B⊕Cin. The carry is 1 for counts 2 and 3, which is the majority. In the two-half-adder build, the first half adder gives A⊕B and the carry A·B, and the second adds Cin to that sum. The two carries can never be 1 at the same time, so an OR combines them. For a multi-bit adder, bit i uses carry C_i from bit i−1, and the top carry-out becomes the extra bit of the answer. For a subtractor the same cells are used with B inverted and Cin = 1 (card a4).

examples.setup: Add A = 101 (5) and B = 011 (3) with three full adders in a row, bit 0 first. Each full adder gives S = A⊕B⊕Cin and Cout = A·B + Cin·(A⊕B). The first Cin is 0.
steps: Line up the bits. Bit 0 is on the left of the picture: A = 1, 0, 1 and B = 1, 1, 0 from bit 0 to bit 2. The first carry-in is 0.
Read the result from the top: C3 S2 S1 S0 = 1 0 0 0 = 8. Check: 5 + 3 = 8.
examples.answer: Sum = 1000 = 8. Each full adder passes its carry-out to the next stage's carry-in.

examples.setup: A full adder is built from two half adders and an OR gate. An XOR gate takes 4 ns, an AND or OR gate 2 ns. A, B and Cin are all ready at t = 0. When are S and Cout ready, and what is the Cin to Cout delay?
steps: HA1 (A, B): S1 = A⊕B is ready at 4 ns, C1 = A·B at 2 ns.
HA2 (S1, Cin): S = S1⊕Cin is ready at 4 + 4 = 8 ns, and C2 = S1·Cin at 4 + 2 = 6 ns.
Cout = C1 + C2 uses the OR gate after the later input: max(2, 6) + 2 = 8 ns.
From Cin alone, Cout needs one AND and one OR: 2 + 2 = 4 ns. This carry-in to carry-out path is what repeats in a ripple adder.
examples.answer: S and Cout are ready at 8 ns. The Cin to Cout delay is 4 ns.

examples.setup: The first stage of an adder has no carry-in (Cin = 0). Show that a full adder with Cin = 0 behaves like a half adder, using A = 1 and B = 1.
steps: Put Cin = 0 in the formulas: S = A⊕B⊕0 = A⊕B and Cout = A·B + 0·(A⊕B) = A·B.
For A = B = 1: S = 1⊕1 = 0 and Cout = 1·1 = 1.
These are exactly the half-adder equations, so the least significant stage can be a half adder. It saves one XOR, one AND and the OR gate.
examples.answer: S = 0 and Cout = 1. With Cin = 0 the full adder reduces to a half adder.

cards.why: The full adder is the building block of every adder and of the ALU. In GATE: find the sum and carry for given inputs, write its equations, or find the delay of a full adder made from simpler gates.
how: Count the ones among A, B and Cin: this gives the sum bit (parity) and the carry (2 or more).
Or compute A⊕B first, then S = (A⊕B)⊕Cin and Cout = AB + Cin(A⊕B).
For an n-bit sum, work from bit 0 and pass each Cout to the next stage.
For delays, add the gate delays along the longest path.
cards.mistake: Writing the carry as A⊕B or the sum as A + B. The carry-out is the majority of the three inputs, not the XOR.
edge_cases: With Cin = 0 a full adder behaves like a half adder.
The carry-out can never be 1 when two of the three inputs are 0.
The final carry-out of the top stage is the extra bit (or the unsigned overflow).
S and Cout are both 1 only when all three inputs are 1.
connections: Half and full adders in dl.comb (card c5) give the same cell from the gate side.
Ripple-carry adder delay (card a2) chains these cells.

cards.title: Ripple-carry adder delay
cards.simple: In a ripple-carry adder the columns are done one after another, because each column needs the carry from the column on its right. It is like a row of dominoes: the last one can fall only when all the ones before it have fallen. If each domino takes 3 ns, six dominoes take about 18 ns, and twice as many columns take twice as long. The worst case is when a carry is created at the first column and passes through every other column. In exam words: ripple-carry delay is linear in n, about n times the carry delay of one stage, and the worst case input makes the carry propagate through all stages.
cards.idea: In a **ripple-carry adder** each stage waits for the carry of the previous one. The delay is **(n − 1) carry stages plus the final sum delay**, linear in n. The worst case is a carry generated at bit 0 that **propagates** through every stage.
cards.definition:
$$T_{ripple}=(n-1)\,t_{carry}+t_{sum}\quad(\approx n\,t_{carry})$$

- $t_{carry}$ = delay from carry-in to carry-out of one full adder.
- $t_{sum}$ = delay from carry-in to sum of the last stage.
- Stage $i$ propagates a carry when $A_i\oplus B_i=1$, and kills it when $A_i=B_i=0$.
cards.intuition_full: Every full adder needs its carry-in before it can finish. The carry-in of stage i is the carry-out of stage i−1, so the carries form a chain, and the delay is the length of that chain. The data decide how long the chain actually is. A stage with A = B = 0 kills the carry, since its carry-out is 0 whatever comes in. A stage with A = B = 1 generates a carry on its own. A stage with exactly one 1 passes the incoming carry on. Timing analysis must assume the worst data, because the clock has to be slow enough for any input. The worst case is a carry made at stage 0 and passed by every other stage, for example A = 00000001 and B = 11111111. The result is a delay that doubles when the width doubles, which is why wide adders use look-ahead (card a3).

examples.setup: A 6-bit ripple-carry adder has six full adders in a row. A carry takes 3 ns to pass through a stage, and a sum bit appears 4 ns after its carry-in arrives. All A and B bits and the first Cin are ready at t = 0. In the worst case, when is the last carry-out ready, and when is the last sum bit ready?
steps: Stage 0 has Cin ready at 0, so its carry-out C1 is ready at 0 + 3 = 3 ns.
Stage 1 needs C1 (3 ns), so C2 is ready at 3 + 3 = 6 ns.
Stage 2: C3 is ready at 6 + 3 = 9 ns.
Stage 3: C4 is ready at 9 + 3 = 12 ns.
Stage 4: C5 is ready at 12 + 3 = 15 ns.
Stage 5 gets C5 at 15 ns. Its carry-out C6 is ready at 15 + 3 = 18 ns. Its sum bit S5 appears 4 ns after the carry-in: 15 + 4 = 19 ns.
The whole adder is ready at 19 ns. The delay is (n − 1) carry stages plus one sum delay, so it grows in proportion to the number of bits.
examples.answer: Last carry-out at 18 ns, last sum bit at 19 ns, so the adder needs 19 ns.

examples.setup: For a ripple adder with t_carry = 3 ns and t_sum = 4 ns, find the worst-case delay for 16 bits and for 32 bits, and compare.
steps: Formula: T = (n − 1) × t_carry + t_sum.
The ratio 97 ÷ 49 is almost 2: doubling the width roughly doubles the delay.

The clock period must work for every input, including inputs like A = 0001 and B = 1111 that make the carry run through all stages. So the design is timed for the worst case.

edge_cases: If t_sum is shorter than t_carry, the last carry-out may be the slowest signal.

cards.title: Carry lookahead
cards.simple: A ripple adder passes the bucket from person to person. A look-ahead adder uses a smart planner who looks at everyone's bits first and decides for each column whether it will make a carry, pass a carry, or stop one. 'Make' is G, which is true when both bits are 1. 'Pass' is P, which is true when exactly one bit is 1. With those two flags every column's carry-in can be written down straight away, without waiting for the columns to its right. The extra planning gates cost area, but the delay no longer grows column by column. In exam words: G = AB and P = A⊕B; C(i+1) = Gi + Pi·Ci expanded gives each carry as a two-level AND-OR of G, P and C0, so the delay is constant (log n with fan-in 2).
cards.idea: **Generate** G = A·B (this bit makes a carry) and **propagate** P = A⊕B (this bit passes a carry on). Then C(i+1) = Gi + Pi·Ci. Expanding it gives every carry directly from G, P and C0, so the **delay no longer grows with n**.
cards.definition:
$$G_i=A_iB_i,\quad P_i=A_i\oplus B_i,\quad C_{i+1}=G_i+P_iC_i,\quad S_i=P_i\oplus C_i$$

Expanded: $C_1=G_0+P_0C_0$, $C_2=G_1+P_1G_0+P_1P_0C_0$, $C_3=G_2+P_2G_1+P_2P_1G_0+P_2P_1P_0C_0$.

Carry $C_k$ needs $k$ AND gates (the lone $G$ term needs none) and one OR gate.
cards.intuition_full: Unroll the recurrence C(i+1) = Gi + Pi·Ci. The carry out of bit i appears if bit i generates it, or if bit i propagates a carry that arrived. That carry-in is itself either generated by bit i−1 or propagated through it, and so on down to C0. Writing this out gives a sum of products with a term for each place the carry could have started. Because the expanded formula has only G, P and C0 as inputs, all carries are ready after the same two gate levels (AND then OR), and none waits for another. The cost is hardware: C_k needs gates with up to k+1 inputs. With fan-in limited to 2 the AND and OR levels become trees of depth log₂ n, giving Θ(log n). Large adders therefore build 4-bit look-ahead blocks and chain or tree them. The sum bit is the XOR of P with the carry into that bit.

examples.setup: Add A = 1011 (11) and B = 0110 (6) with a 4-bit carry look-ahead adder, C0 = 0. Compute G, P, every carry and the sum.
steps: Write the bits, bit 3 on the left. A = 1, 0, 1, 1 and B = 0, 1, 1, 0.
Compute G = A·B and P = A⊕B for every bit at once. Bit 3: G = 0, P = 1. Bit 2: G = 0, P = 1. Bit 1: G = 1, P = 0. Bit 0: G = 0, P = 1.
All carries come from G, P and C0 with C(i+1) = Gi + Pi·Ci: C1 = G0 + P0·C0 = 0. C2 = G1 + P1·C1 = 1. C3 = G2 + P2·C2 = 0 + 1·1 = 1. C4 = G3 + P3·C3 = 0 + 1·1 = 1.
Sum bits S = P⊕C (C = carry into that bit): S0 = 1⊕0 = 1, S1 = 0⊕0 = 0, S2 = 1⊕1 = 0, S3 = 1⊕1 = 0.
Result: C4 S3 S2 S1 S0 = 1 0001 = 17 = 11 + 6. In hardware G and P take one gate level, each carry two more (AND, OR) and the sum one XOR, for any number of bits.
examples.answer: Sum = 10001 = 17, with all carries known after the same few gate levels.

examples.setup: In a 4-bit look-ahead adder, AND and OR gates take 1 time unit and an XOR gate takes 2 units. The inputs A, B and C0 are ready at t = 0. When is the last sum bit ready, using the two-level carry network?
steps: G = A·B takes 1 unit. P = A⊕B takes 2 units. G and P are ready by t = 2.
Each carry is a two-level AND-OR of G, P and C0: AND (1) then OR (1) after t = 2, so all carries are ready at t = 4.
S = P⊕C takes 2 more units, so the last sum is ready at t = 6.
examples.answer: 6 time units, whatever the number of bits (for unlimited fan-in).

examples.setup: A designer expands C4 for a 4-bit adder. Count the AND and OR gates in two-level form, and compare with C3.
steps: C4 = G3 + P3G2 + P3P2G1 + P3P2P1G0 + P3P2P1P0C0. Five terms.
The lone term G3 is a wire. The other four terms are products of two or more literals: 4 AND gates, with 2, 3, 4 and 5 inputs.
One 5-input OR gate joins the terms.
C3 needs 3 ANDs and C4 needs 4 ANDs. Carry Ck needs k AND gates and one OR.
examples.answer: C4: 4 AND gates and 1 OR gate. The widest gate has 5 inputs, so look-ahead trades gate size for speed.

cards.why: Look-ahead is the standard fast adder, and its delay and gate counts are classic GATE material. In GATE: compute G, P and carries for given numbers, write the carry expression, or count gates and delay.
how: Compute Gi = AiBi and Pi = Ai⊕Bi for every bit.
Compute carries in order with C(i+1) = Gi + Pi·Ci (in hardware, all at once).
Sum bits are Si = Pi⊕Ci.
For delay: gate level of G/P, plus two levels per carry, plus one XOR for the sum.
cards.mistake: Counting the lone G term as an AND gate, or adding a full-adder delay per bit for look-ahead. Look-ahead has a fixed depth, not one per bit.
edge_cases: P = A + B (OR) also works for the carry, but the sum then needs A⊕B⊕C.
With fan-in 2 gates the depth becomes log₂ n instead of constant.
A carry that starts at bit j is generated by Gj and then propagated by Pj+1 … Pi.
If XOR is slower than AND/OR, include its larger delay on the critical path.
connections: Ripple delay (card a2) is the linear case that look-ahead replaces.
Add/subtract (card a4) can use a look-ahead adder inside.
dl.comb (card c6) shows the same expansion from the gate side.

cards.title: Add, subtract, overflow and flags
cards.simple: A calculator that holds only 4-bit numbers runs out of room. Signed 4-bit numbers go from −8 to 7. If you add two big positive numbers and the answer would be 9, the display wraps round and shows a negative number. That wrong wrap is called overflow. You can spot it: adding two positives and getting a negative, or two negatives and getting a positive, is always overflow. Mixed signs can never overflow. To subtract, the adder flips the bits of the second number and adds 1, because that gives the negative of the number. In exam words: A − B = A + B' + 1; signed overflow is V = C(n−1) ⊕ Cn, or same-sign inputs with a different-sign result; the carry-out is the unsigned overflow flag.
cards.idea: **Subtraction** uses the adder: A − B = A + B' + 1. **Signed overflow** happens when two numbers of the same sign give a result of the opposite sign: **V = C(n−1) ⊕ C(n)**. The **carry-out** is a different thing: it flags unsigned overflow.
cards.definition:
$$A-B=A+\bar B+1,\qquad V=C_{n-1}\oplus C_n,\qquad V=A_{n-1}B_{n-1}\bar S_{n-1}+\bar A_{n-1}\bar B_{n-1}S_{n-1}$$

- $C_n$ = carry out of the top bit, $C_{n-1}$ = carry into it.
- n-bit two's complement range: $-2^{n-1}\dots 2^{n-1}-1$.
- Positive plus negative never overflows.
cards.intuition_full: Two's complement makes the same adder work for signed and unsigned numbers. The bits of the sum are identical either way, so the difference is in how we judge the result. For unsigned numbers the sum is wrong if a carry leaves the top bit. For signed numbers the sum is wrong if the result has a sign that cannot be right: two positives cannot add to a negative, two negatives cannot add to a positive. These two conditions are separate: −1 + −1 = −2 has a carry-out (1111 + 1111) but no overflow, while 6 + 7 has no carry-out but overflows. The XOR rule V = C(n−1) ⊕ Cn catches exactly the signed case. Subtraction reuses the adder because −B = B' + 1, so the adder gets inverted B and a carry-in of 1. The same circuit gives both operations with an XOR gate on B (dl.comb card c10).

examples.setup: Add A = 1010 (−6) and B = 1011 (−5) in 4-bit two's complement. Find the 4-bit result, the carry-out C4, the carry into the sign bit C3, and decide whether signed overflow occurred.
steps: The true sum is −6 + (−5) = −11, which is outside the 4-bit range −8 to 7. Line up the bits, bit 3 on the left.
Bit 0: 0 + 1 = 1, carry 0. Bit 1: 1 + 1 = 0, carry 1.
Bit 2: 0 + 0 + 1 = 1, carry 0. Bit 3: 1 + 1 + 0 = 0, carry 1. The 4-bit result is 0101 = +5.
Both inputs are negative and the result is positive, so signed overflow occurred. Formula: V = C3 ⊕ C4 = 0 ⊕ 1 = 1, where C3 is the carry into the sign bit and C4 the carry out of it.
The carry-out C4 = 1 is the unsigned flag: as unsigned numbers 10 + 11 = 21 does not fit in 4 bits. Signed overflow is V, not the carry-out. Subtraction uses A + B' + 1 with the same V rule.
examples.answer: Result 0101 with C4 = 1 and V = 1: signed overflow. The carry-out and V can differ.

Bit 0: 0 + 0 + 1 = 1, carry 0. Bit 1: 1 + 1 + 0 = 0, carry 1. Bit 2: 1 + 0 + 1 = 0, carry 1. Bit 3: 0 + 0 + 1 = 1, carry 0.
Result 1001 = −7. But 6 − (−3) = 9, which is outside the range −8 to 7.
V = C3 ⊕ C4 = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1: signed overflow. The result is wrong.
examples.answer: Result 1001 (−7) is wrong; V = 1 flags the overflow.

The result is 1110 = −2, which is correct. C3 = 1 and C4 = 1.
V = C3 ⊕ C4 = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0: no signed overflow, although the carry-out is 1.
examples.answer: Carry-out 1, overflow 0. Do not call the carry-out of the top bit the overflow for signed numbers.

cards.title: ALU structure and flags
cards.simple: An ALU is a box that does arithmetic and logic. You feed it two numbers and an operation code, like ADD or AND, and it gives back an answer. Next to the answer it also gives four small flags that describe it: N says the answer is negative, Z says it is zero, C says a carry left the top, and V says the signed answer overflowed. The CPU does not need a separate compare circuit: it subtracts, throws the answer away, and reads the flags. Which flags to read depends on whether the numbers are signed or unsigned. In exam words: the ALU selects among adder and logic results and reports N, Z, C, V; for A − B, signed A < B is N ⊕ V and unsigned A < B is C = 0 (borrow).
cards.idea: An **ALU** selects one of several results (add, subtract, AND, OR…) and reports **flags**: **N** (negative), **Z** (zero), **C** (carry out), **V** (signed overflow). Comparing A and B is done by subtracting and reading the flags.
cards.definition:
Flags after the operation:

- $N$ = result sign bit, $Z=1$ iff the result is all zeros.
- $C$ = carry out of the top bit, $V=C_{n-1}\oplus C_n$.

Comparison after $A-B$:

- Signed: $A<B \iff N\oplus V=1$. Equal: $Z=1$.
- Unsigned: $A<B \iff C=0$ (borrow). Equal: $Z=1$.
cards.intuition_full: The ALU has one adder and a few extra gates. A multiplexer on the output picks the adder result or a logic result according to the operation code. A comparison is just a subtraction whose result is ignored, and the information about A and B is left behind in the flags. For signed numbers the sign of A − B tells the order only when no overflow happened. If V = 1 the sign bit is wrong, so the true sign is N ⊕ V. For unsigned numbers the sign bit means nothing. Instead, the carry-out of A + B' + 1 is 1 exactly when A ≥ B (no borrow). That is why different branch instructions (signed less-than, unsigned less-than) test different flag combinations. A plain N flag alone is a trap after overflow.

examples.setup: A 4-bit ALU computes A − B for A = 0011 (3) and B = 0110 (6) as A + B' + 1. Find the result and the flags N, Z, C and V, and decide whether A < B for signed and for unsigned numbers.
steps: Subtract by adding the inverted B and a carry-in of 1. The ALU gets A = 0011 and B' = 1001 with the operation SUB.
Result: 0011 + 1001 + 1 = 1101. This is 13 as an unsigned number and −3 as a signed number. The carry out of the top bit is 0.
N is the sign bit of the result: N = 1. Z is 1 only when the result is all zeros: Z = 0.
C is the carry out of the top bit: C = 0. V = C3 ⊕ C4 = 0 ⊕ 0 = 0, so there is no signed overflow.
Signed A < B exactly when N ⊕ V = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1: true, since 3 < 6. For unsigned numbers A < B when a borrow occurred, which is C = 0: also true.
examples.answer: Result 1101 with N = 1, Z = 0, C = 0, V = 0. A < B is true for both signed and unsigned.

examples.setup: A 4-bit ALU computes A − B for A = 0111 (7) and B = 1100 (−4 signed, 12 unsigned). Find N, C, V, and decide whether A < B signed and unsigned. Why is N alone not enough?

Signed: N ⊕ V = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0, so A < B is false. Indeed 7 > −4.
Unsigned: C = 0 (a borrow), so A < B is true. Indeed 7 < 12.
N alone says 'negative', which would claim 7 < −4: wrong after overflow.
examples.answer: N = 1, C = 0, V = 1. Signed 7 < −4 is false; unsigned 7 < 12 is true.

steps: B' = 1010. Compute 0101 + 1010 + 1 = 10000: result 0000, carry out 1.
Z = 1 (all zeros). N = 0. C = 1 (no borrow, A ≥ B). V = 0.
Equality is detected by Z = 1; C = 1 and N ⊕ V = 0 together say A ≥ B.

cards.title: Booth multiplication
cards.simple: Normal binary multiplication adds a shifted copy of the multiplicand for every 1 in the multiplier. A long run of ones, like 0111100, is a lot of adding. Booth noticed that a run of ones is the same as 'subtract once at the start of the run and add once just after the end'. So it looks at pairs of neighbouring bits of the multiplier. When the bits change from 0 to 1 (going up the number) it subtracts, when they change back it adds, and in the middle of a run or a run of zeros it just shifts. It also handles negative multipliers automatically. In exam words: Booth examines (qi, qi−1); 10 subtracts the multiplicand, 01 adds it, 00 and 11 only shift; the shift is arithmetic and the product is 2n bits wide.
cards.idea: **Booth's algorithm** multiplies signed numbers. In each cycle it looks at the pair (Q0, q₋₁): **10 → subtract M, 01 → add M, 00 or 11 → nothing**. Then it shifts A, Q, q₋₁ right **arithmetically**. After n cycles the 2n-bit product is in AQ.
cards.definition:
Registers: $A$ (n bits), $Q$ (multiplier), $q_{-1}$ (extra bit, starts at 0), $M$ (multiplicand).

| $Q_0\,q_{-1}$ | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 0 | $A\leftarrow A-M$ |
| 0 1 | $A\leftarrow A+M$ |
| 0 0 or 1 1 | none |

Then arithmetic shift right of $A,Q,q_{-1}$. Repeat $n$ times. Product $=AQ$ ($2n$ bits).
cards.intuition_full: A multiplier bit string equals the sum over its bits of qᵢ·2ⁱ. A block of ones from bit j to bit k equals 2^(k+1) − 2^j: one subtraction at the low end and one addition above the high end. The pair (qi, qi−1) detects the ends of blocks. A pair 10 means a block of ones starts here (reading from the low end): subtract. A pair 01 means the block just ended: add. Inside a block (11) or a run of zeros (00) nothing is needed. The sign bit is handled by the same rule, because the top bit carries weight −2ⁿ⁻¹ in two's complement and the block ending at the sign bit gets its subtraction. The right shift is arithmetic, which copies the sign bit, so that partial products keep their sign. Booth does the fewest operations when the multiplier has long runs of equal bits.

examples.setup: Multiply M = 0110 (6) by Q = 1011 (−5) with Booth's algorithm on 4-bit registers A, Q and an extra bit q₋₁. Start with A = 0000 and q₋₁ = 0. In each cycle look at (Q0, q₋₁): 10 means A ← A − M, 01 means A ← A + M, 00 and 11 mean no change. Then shift A, Q, q₋₁ right arithmetically.
steps: Start: M = 0110, A = 0000, Q = 1011, q₋₁ = 0. Four cycles are needed, one per bit of Q.
Cycle 2: (1, 1), no add or subtract. Shift right: A = 1110, Q = 1010, q₋₁ = 1.
Cycle 3: (0, 1), add. A = 1110 + 0110 = 0100 (the carry out is dropped). Shift right: A = 0010, Q = 0101, q₋₁ = 0.
Cycle 4: (1, 0), subtract. A = 0010 − 0110 = 1100. Shift right: A = 1110, Q = 0010, q₋₁ = 1.
The product is A Q = 1110 0010, an 8-bit two's complement number = −30. Check: 6 × (−5) = −30.
examples.answer: Product = 11100010 = −30. Booth did 3 add or subtract steps for this multiplier.

examples.setup: How many additions and subtractions does Booth's algorithm perform for the 8-bit multiplier Q = 01101110? Add q₋₁ = 0 on the right and count pair changes.
steps: Write Q with q₋₁ = 0 on its right: Q = 0 1 1 0 1 1 1 0 and q₋₁ = 0. Booth looks at the pair (qi, qi−1) for i = 0 to 7.
Subtract (pair 10) occurs at i = 1 and i = 5, so 2 subtractions. Add (pair 01) occurs at i = 4 and i = 7, so 2 additions. Total 4 operations.
examples.answer: 2 subtractions and 2 additions, 4 operations in all. Count transitions, not ones.

examples.setup: Multiply M = 3 by Q = 1111 (−1) with 4-bit Booth. How many add or subtract steps, and what is the product?
steps: Cycles 2, 3, 4: the pair is (1, 1), so only shifts. After the shifts A Q = 1111 1101.
1111 1101 as an 8-bit two's complement number is −3.
examples.answer: One subtraction only. Product = −3 = 3 × (−1).

After each cycle shift A, Q, q₋₁ right arithmetically (keep the sign bit of A).
After n cycles the product is AQ, 2n bits. Count operations by counting bit changes in Q.

example.setup: Multiply M = 0110 (6) by Q = 1011 (−5) with Booth's algorithm on 4-bit registers A, Q and an extra bit q₋₁. Start with A = 0000 and q₋₁ = 0. In each cycle look at (Q0, q₋₁): 10 means A ← A − M, 01 means A ← A + M, 00 and 11 mean no change. Then shift A, Q, q₋₁ right arithmetically.
steps: Start: M = 0110, A = 0000, Q = 1011, q₋₁ = 0. Four cycles are needed, one per bit of Q.
Cycle 2: (1, 1), no add or subtract. Shift right: A = 1110, Q = 1010, q₋₁ = 1.
Cycle 3: (0, 1), add. A = 1110 + 0110 = 0100 (the carry out is dropped). Shift right: A = 0010, Q = 0101, q₋₁ = 0.

example.answer: Product = 11100010 = −30. Booth did 3 add or subtract steps for this multiplier.

cards.what: **Booth's algorithm** multiplies signed numbers. In each cycle it looks at the pair (Q0, q₋₁): **10 → subtract M, 01 → add M, 00 or 11 → nothing**. Then it shifts A, Q, q₋₁ right **arithmetically**. After n cycles the 2n-bit product is in AQ.
cards.what_full:
**Booth's algorithm** multiplies signed numbers. In each cycle it looks at the pair (Q0, q₋₁): **10 → subtract M, 01 → add M, 00 or 11 → nothing**. Then it shifts A, Q, q₋₁ right **arithmetically**. After n cycles the 2n-bit product is in AQ.

Registers: $A$ (n bits), $Q$ (multiplier), $q_{-1}$ (extra bit, starts at 0), $M$ (multiplicand).

| $Q_0\,q_{-1}$ | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 0 | $A\leftarrow A-M$ |
| 0 1 | $A\leftarrow A+M$ |
| 0 0 or 1 1 | none |

Then arithmetic shift right of $A,Q,q_{-1}$. Repeat $n$ times. Product $=AQ$ ($2n$ bits).

**Worked example.** Multiply M = 0110 (6) by Q = 1011 (−5) with Booth's algorithm on 4-bit registers A, Q and an extra bit q₋₁. Start with A = 0000 and q₋₁ = 0. In each cycle look at (Q0, q₋₁): 10 means A ← A − M, 01 means A ← A + M, 00 and 11 mean no change. Then shift A, Q, q₋₁ right arithmetically.

1. Start: M = 0110, A = 0000, Q = 1011, q₋₁ = 0. Four cycles are needed, one per bit of Q.
2. Cycle 1: (Q0, q₋₁) = (1, 0), subtract. A = 0000 − 0110 = 1010. Shift right: A = 1101, Q = 0101, q₋₁ = 1.
3. Cycle 2: (1, 1), no add or subtract. Shift right: A = 1110, Q = 1010, q₋₁ = 1.
4. Cycle 3: (0, 1), add. A = 1110 + 0110 = 0100 (the carry out is dropped). Shift right: A = 0010, Q = 0101, q₋₁ = 0.
5. Cycle 4: (1, 0), subtract. A = 0010 − 0110 = 1100. Shift right: A = 1110, Q = 0010, q₋₁ = 1.
6. The product is A Q = 1110 0010, an 8-bit two's complement number = −30. Check: 6 × (−5) = −30.

**Answer:** Product = 11100010 = −30. Booth did 3 add or subtract steps for this multiplier.

cards.title: Floating-point arithmetic
cards.simple: Floating point is scientific notation in binary. Instead of writing 29 you write 1.8125 × 2⁴: a number between 1 and 2, times a power of two. The computer stores three things: whether the number is negative (1 bit), the power (8 bits, with 127 added so it can be stored without a minus sign), and the digits after the leading 1 (23 bits). The leading 1 is not stored because it is always there. To add two such numbers you first shift the smaller one so the powers match, then add the digits, then tidy up so it is again between 1 and 2. To multiply, you add the powers and multiply the digits. In exam words: IEEE single precision is 1 sign, 8 exponent (bias 127) and 23 fraction bits; add = align, add, normalise; multiply = add the exponents and subtract the bias once, multiply the significands.
cards.idea: **IEEE 754 single:** 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits (bias 127), 23 fraction bits. Value = (−1)^s × 1.fraction × 2^(e − 127). **Add:** align exponents, add significands, normalise. **Multiply:** add exponents (subtract the bias once), multiply significands.
cards.definition:
$$x=(-1)^s\times(1.f)_2\times 2^{\,e-127}\qquad(0<e<255)$$

- $s$ = sign bit, $e$ = biased exponent field, $f$ = 23 fraction bits.
- Addition: shift the smaller number right until exponents match, add, normalise.
- Multiplication: $e_{result}=e_1+e_2-127$ and significands multiply.
- $e=0$ gives zero or denormals; $e=255$ gives infinity or NaN.
cards.intuition_full: A fixed-point format wastes bits on a range that you rarely need. Floating point stores the order of magnitude (the exponent) separately from the precision (the fraction), so the same 32 bits cover tiny and huge numbers. The bias makes the exponent field an unsigned number while the true exponent can be negative. The leading 1 is implicit because after normalisation the significand always starts with 1, so storing it would waste a bit. Addition needs matching exponents because only digits of the same weight can be added. The smaller number loses low bits when shifted right, which is where rounding comes from. In multiplication the exponents add, but each stored field contains the bias, so adding the two fields counts the bias twice and one 127 must be subtracted. After either operation the result is normalised again by shifting the significand and adjusting the exponent.

examples.setup: Decode the IEEE 754 single-precision word 0x41E80000. The layout is 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits (bias 127) and 23 fraction bits, with an implicit leading 1.
steps: Write 0x41E80000 in binary: 0100 0001 1110 1000 0000 … Split into 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits and 23 fraction bits: 0 | 10000011 | 11010000000000000000000.
The sign bit is 0, so the number is positive.
The exponent field 10000011 is 131. Subtract the bias 127: the true exponent is 131 − 127 = 4.
The fraction 1101 followed by zeros has an implicit leading 1, so the significand is 1.1101 in binary = 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/16 = 1.8125.

examples.setup: Add 1.375 × 2⁵ and 1.5 × 2³. Align, add and normalise.
steps: The larger exponent is 5. Shift the smaller number right by 5 − 3 = 2 places: 1.5 × 2³ = 0.375 × 2⁵.
Add the significands: 1.375 + 0.375 = 1.75.
1.75 is already between 1 and 2, so no normalisation shift is needed. The result is 1.75 × 2⁵.

examples.setup: Multiply a = 1.75 × 2³ (biased exponent 130) by b = 1.5 × 2⁻² (biased exponent 125). A student adds the exponent fields. What goes wrong, and what is the correct product?
steps: The student gets 130 + 125 = 255, which is the code for infinity or NaN. This counts the bias twice.
Correct: e = 130 + 125 − 127 = 128, so the true exponent is 128 − 127 = 1.
Significands: 1.75 × 1.5 = 2.625, which is 2 or more, so normalise: 2.625 = 1.3125 × 2. The exponent rises by 1 to 2, and the biased field becomes 129.
examples.answer: Biased exponent 129, value 5.25. Subtract the bias once, then normalise.

scenes.title: Adding 101 and 011 with three full adders

steps.caption: Line up the bits. Bit 0 is on the left of the picture: A = 1, 0, 1 and B = 1, 1, 0 from bit 0 to bit 2. The first carry-in is 0.
Read the result from the top: C3 S2 S1 S0 = 1 0 0 0 = 8. Check: 5 + 3 = 8.

scenes.title: The carry crosses six stages, 3 ns each

objects.text: carry-out time in ns (3 ns per stage)

steps.caption: Stage 0 has Cin ready at 0, so its carry-out C1 is ready at 0 + 3 = 3 ns.
Stage 1 needs C1 (3 ns), so C2 is ready at 3 + 3 = 6 ns.
Stage 2: C3 is ready at 6 + 3 = 9 ns.
Stage 3: C4 is ready at 9 + 3 = 12 ns.
Stage 4: C5 is ready at 12 + 3 = 15 ns.
Stage 5 gets C5 at 15 ns. Its carry-out C6 is ready at 15 + 3 = 18 ns. Its sum bit S5 appears 4 ns after the carry-in: 15 + 4 = 19 ns.
The whole adder is ready at 19 ns. The delay is (n − 1) carry stages plus one sum delay, so it grows in proportion to the number of bits.

scenes.title: Look-ahead: G and P first, then every carry at once

steps.caption: Write the bits, bit 3 on the left. A = 1, 0, 1, 1 and B = 0, 1, 1, 0.
Compute G = A·B and P = A⊕B for every bit at once. Bit 3: G = 0, P = 1. Bit 2: G = 0, P = 1. Bit 1: G = 1, P = 0. Bit 0: G = 0, P = 1.
All carries come from G, P and C0 with C(i+1) = Gi + Pi·Ci: C1 = G0 + P0·C0 = 0. C2 = G1 + P1·C1 = 1. C3 = G2 + P2·C2 = 0 + 1·1 = 1. C4 = G3 + P3·C3 = 0 + 1·1 = 1.
Sum bits S = P⊕C (C = carry into that bit): S0 = 1⊕0 = 1, S1 = 0⊕0 = 0, S2 = 1⊕1 = 0, S3 = 1⊕1 = 0.
Result: C4 S3 S2 S1 S0 = 1 0001 = 17 = 11 + 6. In hardware G and P take one gate level, each carry two more (AND, OR) and the sum one XOR, for any number of bits.

scenes.title: Adding two negatives: the sign flips, V = 1

objects.text: C4 = 1 is the unsigned flag, not overflow

steps.caption: The true sum is −6 + (−5) = −11, which is outside the 4-bit range −8 to 7. Line up the bits, bit 3 on the left.
Bit 0: 0 + 1 = 1, carry 0. Bit 1: 1 + 1 = 0, carry 1.
Bit 2: 0 + 0 + 1 = 1, carry 0. Bit 3: 1 + 1 + 0 = 0, carry 1. The 4-bit result is 0101 = +5.
Both inputs are negative and the result is positive, so signed overflow occurred. Formula: V = C3 ⊕ C4 = 0 ⊕ 1 = 1, where C3 is the carry into the sign bit and C4 the carry out of it.
The carry-out C4 = 1 is the unsigned flag: as unsigned numbers 10 + 11 = 21 does not fit in 4 bits. Signed overflow is V, not the carry-out. Subtraction uses A + B' + 1 with the same V rule.

scenes.title: ALU subtract: result and flags N Z C V

objects.text: signed: N xor V = 1, so A < B

steps.caption: Subtract by adding the inverted B and a carry-in of 1. The ALU gets A = 0011 and B' = 1001 with the operation SUB.
Result: 0011 + 1001 + 1 = 1101. This is 13 as an unsigned number and −3 as a signed number. The carry out of the top bit is 0.
N is the sign bit of the result: N = 1. Z is 1 only when the result is all zeros: Z = 0.
C is the carry out of the top bit: C = 0. V = C3 ⊕ C4 = 0 ⊕ 0 = 0, so there is no signed overflow.
Signed A < B exactly when N ⊕ V = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1: true, since 3 < 6. For unsigned numbers A < B when a borrow occurred, which is C = 0: also true.
